data.title: Middle East Eye: Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
data.author: Yasmine El-Sabawi
data.summary:
Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
Submitted by
Yasmine El-Sabawi
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:11
The country's former and only Islamophobia envoy calls the decision "devastating"
A view of the exterior of the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa, Ontario, on 12 July 2017 (Creative Commons)
Off
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld Quebec's highly contested 2019 law that bans religious symbols in the public sector.
It was, more than anything, seen to be targeting Muslim women in the province who wear the hijab, but also impacted Catholics, Sikhs and other minorities.
Quebec's population is 5 percent Muslim, according to the last census carried out in 2021. That figure is second only to Ontario.
Amira Elghawaby, who was Canada’s first and only special representative on combatting Islamophobia, until her office was shut down earlier this year, called the verdict "devastating".
"The promise of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been broken, and could be broken again and again. It means that religious freedoms, equality and the rights of all Canadians are no longer guaranteed," Elghawaby said in a statement released by the organisation she founded this year, the Muslim Communities Research Observatory.
“This ruling will instantly further impact the lives and livelihoods of Quebecers, particularly Muslim women who wear the hijab. In one study, 71% of Muslim women surveyed had considered leaving Quebec, with the province standing to lose an estimated $3.2 billion in income. It may also open the door for further violations of rights and freedoms," she added.
Technicality
Oftentimes rulings by the highest court come down to technicalities.
What the court was looking at in this case was the application of Section 33 of the constitution, known as the "notwithstanding clause", which shields Bill 21 from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms itself.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, drawing criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday.
Turk said he was "deeply concerned" by Costa Rica's decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose.
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica.
The UN human rights office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on "claimed national security grounds".
The government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts".
An Italian lawyer, Albanese is the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory, which has been occupied by Israel since 1967. She has been sanctioned by the United States since 2025.
"I am deeply indignant that the government of Costa Rica has spread false information that links me to terrorism," Albanese said from the airport, adding that she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision.
Israel's UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica's decision in a post on X.
Under President Laura Fernandez, Costa Rica has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and moved closer to Israel. It signed a free trade agreement with Israel last year.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Eisenkot says Netanyahu dragging out coalition talks as deadline nears
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Eisenkot says Netanyahu dragging out coalition talks as deadline nears
Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli opposition leader who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, said on Friday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been dragging out the negotiations, even though his Yashar Party is willing to agree on key points, Haaretz reported.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
According to Haaretz, sources close to Eisenkot's bloc expect Netanyahu to make a significant offer next week to prevent the government Eisenkot is planning from being sworn in.
Yashar and Likud met five times over the past two weeks to negotiate. Eisenkot said that Likud had refused on several days to schedule meetings as frequently as his party proposed.
"Two weeks and five meetings are a sufficient period in which an agreement could already have been reached, if they had wanted one," he said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli attacks across Gaza kill four Palestinians
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Israeli attacks across Gaza kill four Palestinians
Israeli attacks killed four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Friday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Several others, including a child, were wounded in a series of attacks across the strip.
In the southern city of Rafah, Gaza's civil defence crews recovered three bodies. They also rescued two wounded people after an Israeli strike near the Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, in the west of the city.
Wafa reported earlier on Friday that an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp, killing a Palestinian man and wounding several others, some seriously.
Medical sources and eyewitnesses said Israeli forces stationed near the so-called "Yellow Line" repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the area.
The so-called "Yellow Line" is a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured.

data.author: Sean Mathews
data.summary:
Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 21:00
Oman's economy has emerged as a relative winner amid the Iran war thanks to its geography and diplomacy, experts say
A man views Rasool al-Adham Mosque from the corniche at Port Sultan Qaboos in Oman's capital, Muscat, on 5 February 2026 (Loic Venance/AFP)
Off
Oman’s stock market is on track to be the best performer in the Gulf region in 2026, with its economic growth pulling ahead of neighbours, in a sign of how it is reaping gains from distancing itself from the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The MSX30 Index, which tracks the performance of Oman’s stock exchange, has soared 22 percent year-to-date.
Dubai's stock market, the Dubai Financial Market General Index, the region’s second-best performer, is up 8.7 percent year-to-date. Saudi Arabia’s Tadawul market is down 3 percent year-to-date.
For comparison, in the US, the SP500 index is up 6.4 percent year-to-date after a sharp selloff in AI and technology.
Both the Saudi and Dubai stock markets have clawed back the steep losses of earlier this year after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran.
But Oman's success is more interesting when one considers the anger US President Donald Trump directed at it during negotiations with Iran over the way to manage traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which is comprised of Iran and Oman's territorial waters.
Trump threatened to “blow up” Oman, where his family real estate business has licensed its name for use on a golf resort.
Oman: From outlier to trailblazer
Tensions are still simmering between the US and Iran. The US has launched strikes on Iran and its vessels, while Iran has attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf countries.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Doctors Without Borders says two staff killed in Israeli 'direct hit' on Gaza clinic
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Doctors Without Borders says two staff killed in Israeli 'direct hit' on Gaza clinic
Two employees of Doctors Without Borders (MSF) were killed in an Israeli strike on one of the organisation's clinics in the Gaza Strip on Friday.
The strike was a "direct hit" on the clinic, the organisation said.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight," MSF said in a post on X.
"Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military," it added.
The organisation says these killings bring the number of MSF staff killed by Israel in Gaza to 17.
The attack on the MSF clinic, close to al-Shifa Hospital, brought the death toll from Israeli attacks across the strip on Friday to eight.
Earlier on Friday evening, another Palestinian was shot dead by Israeli forces in the al-Mawasi area, southwest of Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, Wafa news agency reported.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin

Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
Raids and attacks by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank on Friday left at least three Palestinians injured and several detained.
Three Palestinians were injured and another, identified as Muhammad Daifallah Arara, was detained on Friday night after Israeli occupation forces raided his home north of occupied Jerusalem and assaulted those inside.
The three sustained injuries to their shoulders, limbs and abdomens after being beaten by Israeli soldiers, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
Earlier, a group of Israeli settlers attacked the family's home, attempting to break down its entrance and storm its courtyard, before Israeli forces intervened and raided the house.
Israeli forces raided a residential cave in the village of Khirbet Khallat al-Daba'a in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, on Friday evening, assaulting its owner, detaining his family members and vandalising property inside, Wafa news agency reported.
The cave belongs to activist Jaber al-Dababseh, who was beaten by Israeli soldiers while his family members were detained.
On Friday evening, Israeli forces fired tear gas at Palestinian residents in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, during a raid. Israeli soldiers forced shop owners to close their stores.
In the village of Jayyus, east of Qalqilya, Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians after raiding their homes and ransacking their property.
Israeli settlers also continued their attacks across the occupied West Bank throughout the day. They attacked Palestinian vehicles in the Wadi al-Shaer area in the Salfit governorate, damaging at least two, locals told Wafa.
In the town of Za'tara, east of Bethlehem, settlers set up tents, raising fears among Palestinian residents that they could pave the way for a new Israeli outpost there.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Drone that killed two Italians in Kuwait was Iranian-made, says Italy's foreign minister
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Drone that killed two Italians in Kuwait was Iranian-made, says Italy's foreign minister
The drone used in the attack on Kuwait that killed two Italians was manufactured in Iran, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Friday.
In an interview with the Italian press, Tajani said: "According to the investigations carried out by the Kuwaitis, the drone was manufactured in Iran."
The attack on Thursday also injured two other people.
It drew condemnation from many countries, and some, including Syria and Saudi Arabia, blamed Iran for it.
Meanwhile, Iran has denied launching the drone, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the incident "suspicious".
"The Iranians say it was not launched from Iranian territory, but, as you know, Iran's proxies, all of Iran's allies, have Iranian-made drones," Tajani told press.
"There will be investigations, and the Iranians have said they are ready to participate in a commission of inquiry alongside the Italians and Kuwaitis," he added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: IRGC says two oil tankers catch fire after hitting naval mines
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
IRGC says two oil tankers catch fire after hitting naval mines
Two oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking mines near Oman's Khasab port and in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said.
In a statement carried by Iranian news agency, Irna, the IRGC Navy said one tanker struck a naval mine at the entrance to Khasab Port, while a second tanker travelling along an "unauthorised route" east of the Strait of Hormuz also exploded and caught fire.
"Like the tankers that exploded previously, these vessels were attempting to slip through the Strait of Hormuz undetected via a sham route by disabling their tracking systems. Both ultimately exploded and burned near the southern coastline and Khasab Port," the statement said.

Israeli military claims MSF workers killed in Gaza strike were Hamas members
The Israeli military has said the two Doctors Without Borders (MSF) workers -- Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Ma’ad Yousef Ali Sabeh -- killed in an air strike on a clinic in Gaza City were members of Hamas.
In a statement, the military said Ali Sabeh was as an artillery unit commander in Hamas’s armed wing, without providing any evidence. It denied targeting a hospital or damaging medical infrastructure, saying precautions had been taken to minimise civilian casualties.

Yemeni forces claim 121 Houthi fighters killed in 726 attacks
Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, claimed as many as 726 attacks had been carried against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours.
Al-Nuzaili said the operations, conducted as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 23 air strikes, 642 artillery attacks, 35 drone operations and 26 rocket strikes. They resulted in the killing or wounding 121 fighters and commanders, according to the state-run Saba news agency.
The attacks also destroyed or damaged 81 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, he added.

Houthi attacks kill three civilians and wound three others in Taiz, report says
Houthi attacks in Yemen's Taiz province killed three civilians, including a child, according to the government-run Saba news agency.
Houthi drone strikes, rocket fire and sniper attacks targeted residential areas on Friday, killing three people, including a 10-year-old boy and his father, the report said.
Among the injured was an 18-month-old girl, who was wounded in shelling in the Sabir al-Mawadim district.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli defence minister rejects army chief's call to detain violent settlers, report says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Israeli defence minister rejects army chief's call to detain violent settlers, report says
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has rejected a new request from military chief of staff Eyal Zamir to authorise administrative detention orders against Israeli settlers involved in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, Kan reported.
Zamir told Katz at a security consultation on Thursday that further steps were needed amid rising settler violence, and called for administrative detention and restraining orders against perpetrators, the report said.
Administrative detention allows suspects to be held indefinitely without charge or trial. It is widely used against Palestinians, including children, but Katz halted its use against Jewish Israelis in November 2024. He has, in fact, repeatedly boasted of doing so, while expanding its use against Palestinians.
Dozens of restraining orders, which bar individuals from parts of the West Bank, are awaiting Shin Bet approval, according to Kan. Channel 12 reported that 70 people suspected of involvement in such attacks were arrested in recent weeks, but Israeli courts released all of them without indictments.
Shin Bet chief David Zini, who belongs to the Orthodox nationalist Hardal camp, has consistently objected to movement bans. He has been accused of undermining the agency's unit tasked with tackling settler violence.
